questions.stem: Why does increasing body size make diffusion across an organism’s outer surface less adequate?

options.text: Surface area-to-volume ratio decreases and diffusion distances to internal cells increase
options.why: Less exchange surface is available per unit of tissue, while gases also have farther to travel.

options.text: Surface area and volume both decrease while internal cells consume more oxygen
options.why: Surface area and volume increase as an organism grows. The problem is that volume rises faster than surface area.

options.text: Surface area-to-volume ratio increases and gases leave the surface too rapidly
options.why: The ratio decreases with size. Large organisms have too little outer surface relative to their volume.

options.text: Cell membranes become impermeable to oxygen when organisms contain many cells
options.why: Cell membranes remain permeable to oxygen. Distance and available exchange area create the difficulty.

questions.stem: Which feature of a gas-exchange surface directly reduces diffusion distance?

options.text: A dense capillary network
options.why: Capillary flow helps maintain concentration gradients. It doesn’t make the tissue barrier thinner.

options.text: A thin tissue layer
options.why: A thin barrier shortens the path gas molecules must cross, increasing the diffusion rate.

options.text: A moist surface
options.why: Moisture lets gases dissolve before crossing membranes. Its main effect isn’t shortening the path.

options.text: A large surface area
options.why: A large area lets more molecules cross at once. It doesn’t reduce each molecule’s travel distance.

questions.stem: What is the main role of continuous blood flow beside alveoli?

options.text: It produces surfactant that prevents alveolar collapse
options.why: Type II pneumocytes produce surfactant. Blood flow has a different role in maintaining gradients.

options.text: It forces oxygen across the alveolar wall by active transport
options.why: Oxygen crosses by diffusion, not active transport. Blood flow keeps diffusion favorable.

options.text: It carries exchanged gases away and maintains concentration gradients
options.why: Flow brings oxygen-poor blood and removes oxygenated blood, preventing equilibrium at the surface.

options.text: It ventilates the alveoli by moving air through bronchioles
options.why: Ventilation moves air through the airways. Blood flow occurs on the other side of the exchange surface.

options.text: The diaphragm relaxes, thoracic volume decreases and lung pressure falls
options.why: A relaxed diaphragm contributes to exhalation, and decreasing volume raises pressure rather than lowering it.

options.text: The diaphragm contracts, thoracic volume increases and lung pressure falls
options.why: The pressure falls below atmospheric pressure when thoracic volume increases, so air moves inward.

options.text: The internal intercostal muscles contract, pulling the ribs downward and outward
options.why: Internal intercostals act mainly in forced exhalation and pull the ribs downward and inward.

options.text: The abdominal muscles contract, increasing thoracic volume and drawing air inward
options.why: Abdominal muscle contraction assists forced exhalation by pushing the diaphragm upward and reducing thoracic volume.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes pulmonary surfactant?

options.text: It increases surface tension so alveoli recoil during inhalation
options.why: Surfactant reduces surface tension. Increased surface tension would make alveolar collapse more likely.

options.text: It carries oxygen across the alveolar wall into capillaries
options.why: Oxygen diffuses across the wall without a surfactant carrier. Surfactant stabilizes the alveoli.

options.text: It is secreted by type I pneumocytes to thicken the exchange surface
options.why: Type II pneumocytes secrete it, and a thicker exchange surface would slow diffusion.

options.text: It reduces surface tension and helps prevent alveolar collapse
options.why: It acts at the air-water interface in the alveolar lining, helping keep alveoli open.

questions.stem: A person exhales as deeply as possible after taking the deepest possible breath. Which volume has been measured?

options.text: Tidal volume
options.why: Tidal volume is the air moved during one normal resting breath.

options.text: Vital capacity
options.why: Vital capacity is the greatest volume exhaled after the deepest possible inhalation.

options.text: Expiratory reserve
options.why: Expiratory reserve is only the extra volume exhaled after a normal exhalation.

options.text: Residual volume
options.why: Residual volume remains in the lungs after maximal exhalation and can’t be breathed into the measuring device.

questions.stem: Why does opening stomata for carbon dioxide uptake also increase water loss?

options.text: Guard cells actively pump water vapor from xylem into the atmosphere
options.why: Water vapor leaves by diffusion. Guard cells regulate pore width rather than pumping vapor.

options.text: Carbon dioxide reacts with water and converts it directly into vapor
options.why: Carbon dioxide uptake doesn’t convert liquid water into vapor. Evaporation occurs from moist mesophyll walls.

options.text: Water vapor diffuses out through the same open pores used for gas exchange
options.why: Evaporation fills the leaf air spaces with water vapor, which then diffuses through open stomata.

options.text: Open stomata remove the waxy cuticle from the entire lower epidermis
options.why: Opening a stoma changes the guard cells around one pore. It doesn’t remove the surrounding cuticle.

questions.stem: Which change would generally decrease transpiration while the other conditions remain constant?

options.text: An increase in wind speed
options.why: Wind removes the humid boundary layer, maintaining a steeper water-vapor gradient and increasing transpiration.

options.text: An increase in air humidity
options.why: Humid air reduces the water-vapor concentration gradient between the leaf and its surroundings.

options.text: An increase in temperature
options.why: Higher temperature generally increases evaporation and steepens the water-vapor gradient.

options.text: An increase in light intensity
options.why: Greater light commonly promotes stomatal opening for photosynthesis, increasing water loss.

questions.stem: A microscope field with an area of 0.20 mm² contains a mean of 16 stomata. What is the stomatal density?

options.text: 3.2 stomata mm⁻²
options.why: This comes from multiplying count by area. Density requires division by the area examined.

options.text: 16 stomata mm⁻²
options.why: That reports the count as though the field covered one square millimeter, but it covered only 0.20 mm².

options.text: 80 stomata mm⁻²
options.why: Divide the mean count by field area: 16 ÷ 0.20 mm² gives 80 stomata mm⁻².

options.text: 320 stomata mm⁻²
options.why: This value divides by 0.05 rather than the stated field area of 0.20 mm².

questions.stem: Why is the haemoglobin oxygen dissociation curve sigmoid?

options.text: Each bound oxygen molecule increases affinity for the next through a conformational change
options.why: Cooperative binding produces slow initial binding, a steep middle region and a plateau near saturation.

options.text: Each haem group binds oxygen independently with the same affinity at every oxygen pressure
options.why: Constant independent affinity would fail to produce the cooperative steepening that gives the curve its sigmoid shape.

options.text: Haemoglobin binds carbon dioxide at low oxygen pressure and converts it into oxygen
options.why: Haemoglobin can bind carbon dioxide, but it can’t convert carbon dioxide into oxygen.

options.text: Oxygen binding becomes weaker after every occupied haem group until saturation occurs
options.why: Early oxygen binding increases the affinity of remaining sites. That positive cooperation creates the steep section.

questions.stem: How does foetal haemoglobin differ from adult haemoglobin at the same oxygen partial pressure?

options.text: It has lower oxygen affinity and a curve farther to the right
options.why: That would make oxygen uptake from maternal blood harder. Foetal haemoglobin has higher affinity.

options.text: It has higher oxygen affinity and a curve farther to the left
options.why: The higher affinity allows foetal haemoglobin to load oxygen released by maternal haemoglobin at the placenta.

options.text: It has identical oxygen affinity but contains twice as many haem groups
options.why: Foetal and adult haemoglobin each have four haem-containing subunits. Their affinities differ because their globin structures differ.

options.text: It binds carbon dioxide instead of oxygen until the moment of birth
options.why: Foetal haemoglobin transports oxygen before birth. Its key difference here is its higher oxygen affinity.

questions.stem: What does a rightward Bohr shift cause in an actively respiring tissue?

options.text: Greater haemoglobin affinity and reduced oxygen unloading at a given oxygen pressure
options.why: A right shift means lower affinity, not greater affinity, so oxygen unloading increases.

options.text: More oxygen binding because carbon dioxide raises the pH of the blood
options.why: Increased carbon dioxide lowers pH and promotes oxygen release rather than additional binding.

options.text: Reduced oxygen affinity and increased unloading at a given oxygen pressure
options.why: High carbon dioxide and lower pH change haemoglobin’s conformation, delivering more oxygen to active tissue.

options.text: Permanent denaturation of haemoglobin by carbon dioxide produced during respiration
options.why: The affinity change is reversible and regulatory. Haemoglobin hasn’t been permanently denatured.
